name: Sam Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can give me the public version and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior fruit and speciality buyer at Greenmarket Provisions, which supplies about 400 restaurants and cafes. I'm up at 5 to catch growers before they leave for the fields, and I'm at the market floor by 6. Then it's the screen: what's coming, what's cheap, what the chefs want next week. I love the chats with growers and the smell of ripe peaches. I don't love throwing out fruit that turned before it sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful and a bit overpromised, and I'd say it with a shrug. Online I'd probably post about the prompt I wrote that predicts our herb orders, because people love a practical example. Among friends, I'd say don't believe the end-of-the-world stuff, or the utopia stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm happy. I already use AI every day, so a slower world just means my tricks stay a bit of an edge for a few more years. My wife Lucia and I are in good shape, the house is nearly paid and I'm two or three years from stepping back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building little tools. This winter I'd feed three years of order data into a forecasting sheet and see if I can cut our spoilage by a fifth. I'd also train our two juniors to use it, because I'd like to leave them something. And I'd keep ordering for the cafes by gut when the data's silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly, a bit pleased with myself. It feels like a decent game and I'm winning slowly. No dread at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned spoilage. What would you actually do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spoilage is the big one. Last summer we binned about 900 kilos of berries because a heatwave moved the harvest and the orders didn't move with it. If my sheet cuts that even by 15 percent, that's real money for Greenmarket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would success look like for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the owners would give me the credit and I'd take a day off. Mostly I'd tell Lucia and sit in her pottery studio. I already use AI every day, so a slow world just gives me a few more years of being the person who knows the tricks.

say: I'd say it's **useful** and overpromised, and ignore the doom and the utopia.
I'd post a practical example of my herb-order **prompt** online.
think: I'm happy, because I already use AI daily and a slow world keeps my **edge**.
Our house is nearly paid and I'm two or three years from **stepping back**.
do: Feed three years of order data into a **forecasting** sheet this winter.
Train our two **juniors** to use it.
Keep ordering for the cafes by **gut** when the data looks silly.
feel: **Good**, a bit pleased with myself, with no dread at all.
S0.quote: I already use AI every day, so a slow world just gives me a few more years of being the person who knows the tricks.
fieldNote: Sam is already an AI daily user, so a slow world is a comfortable edge, not a threat.
His focus is **spoilage** in perishable stock, a concrete, money-linked target.
Calm is justified by strong savings, a nearly paid house and high skill with the tools.

steps.text: Build a forecasting sheet from three years of order data to cut spoilage
Teach the two junior buyers to use the sheet
Keep ordering by gut for cafes when the data looks silly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to roll up our sleeves. At work I'd tell the owners to buy a proper tool and let me run the pilot. Online I'd say to anyone in desk work: learn it this year, because the people who can check it will be valued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job changes shape. The comparing and the reorder maths go to the machine within two years, and what's left is knowing growers, tasting fruit and knowing which chef will pay for something odd. That's maybe 40 percent of what I do now. I think I'm OK, because I'm already doing that part, but I won't pretend others on the team are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the pilot and write the rules for how Greenmarket uses it, including who checks the machine's orders. I'd move the juniors onto grower visits and chef tastings so they learn the human half. And I'd keep a little of my pay in a side fund, in case the owners decide to pay buyers less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a little guilty. I'm in the fortunate group, and I'd feel odd about that when Dee at accounts, who does invoice checking, is going to see her whole desk disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dee is 52, and so is Hal on the payables desk. Neither of them use anything beyond the basics. I'd offer to teach them on Friday afternoons, and ask the owners to guarantee that nobody's let go within the first year of the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the owners to guarantee, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much in the first year, since the owners have promised nothing. But I'd want it in writing. The comparing and the reorder maths go to the machine, and what's left is knowing growers, tasting fruit and knowing which chef will pay for something odd.

say: I'd tell the owners to buy a proper tool and let me run the **pilot**.
I'd tell desk workers online to learn it this year, since **checking** will be valued.
think: Comparing and reorder maths move to the machine, leaving about **40 percent** of today's job.
I'm in the **fortunate** group, and I feel odd about it.
do: Lead the **pilot** and write rules for who checks the machine's orders.
Move the juniors to grower **visits** and chef tastings.
Put part of my pay into a **side fund** in case buyers' pay drops.
feel: **Excited** and a little guilty, because others on the team will lose desks.
S1.quote: The comparing and the reorder maths go to the machine, and what's left is knowing growers, tasting fruit and knowing which chef will pay for something odd.
fieldNote: Sam is excited rather than anxious: he is adaptive, well-off and sure the human half of buying is his.
He worries for colleagues **Dee and Hal**, who do the checking work AI takes first.
The pilot-lead plan shows he moves first and tries to widen who benefits.

steps.text: Lead the pilot of the buying tool and write rules for checking its orders
Teach Dee and Hal the new tool on Friday afternoons
Move the junior buyers onto grower visits and chef tastings
Put part of my pay into a side fund in case buyers' pay drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing that's ever happened and we're utterly unprepared. At work I'd say let's use the two years to look after the people who will be hit. And online I'd say that the sensible adults had better wake up and plan an income floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my buying job is gone in two years, maybe sooner. The thinking half is automatic, and the grower and chef relationships can be done by a machine that never sleeps and never forgets a birthday. That makes me sad, because it's the part I love. It also makes me curious, a little guiltily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to retire at 60 and take whatever Greenmarket offers. We'd sell the second car, keep the house and put the rest into shares and index funds. I'd spend a year learning to grow things on a small plot, since food is hands-on and the robots are three years behind. And I'd join a campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and awake. Not terrified, because we have money and I'm adaptable, but afraid for everyone I know who doesn't have the cushion we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Marco and Gina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Marco works for the city council in planning, which is thinking work, and our daughter Gina is a chef, which is hands-on. I'd tell Marco to get ready for a very different job, and Gina that she's got a few years' head start. I'd say to both: come to dinner every Sunday, and tell me if you need money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots are three years behind. How does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me a bit more hopeful. The thinking half of my job is automatic and the robots for the hands-on half come three years later, so I'd learn to grow food. I'd sooner have the three years, even so, to see what the world looks like.

say: I'd say this is the **biggest** thing that's ever happened and we're unprepared.
I'd call online for an **income floor** and a plan for the hit people.
think: My buying job is **gone** in two years, maybe sooner, including the grower relationships.
It makes me sad and, guiltily, **curious**.
do: Ask to **retire** at 60 and take any Greenmarket offer.
Move savings into **index funds** and sell the second car.
Learn to **grow** food on a small plot and back a basic income campaign.
feel: **Anxious** and awake, afraid for people without our cushion.
S2.quote: The thinking half of my job is automatic and the robots for the hands-on half come three years later, so I'd learn to grow food.
fieldNote: Sam expects the buying job to go within two years, yet keeps a plan because savings and adaptability give him room.
The quote links the **robot lag** to a hands-on retraining choice, which fits his thinking-heavy job.
His anxiety is mostly empathy for friends and children with less cushion.

steps.text: Ask to retire at 60 and take any Greenmarket package
Move savings into index funds and sell the second car
Learn to grow food on a small plot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say, is time to get ready and I'd say so loudly. At work I'd get a working group going. I'd tell friends who are in office jobs to make a plan with dates in it, not just a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd stay through to the early part of it, maybe retire at 61, and be gone before the hard part. But I'd keep tinkering with the tools so that I'm one of the people who can still explain them to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work another three years, build the forecasting tool properly and train the juniors. I'd start a small consulting job for independent grocers who can't afford a buyer, using the tools, and I'd put money into my kids' house deposit. And I'd take a short fruit-grading course for the fun of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy and a bit excited. It's a slow burn, and I'd feel I was making use of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marco about the next five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: look, it's only five years, but if you're in your twenties you can still switch to something hands-on, or build a business. I'd say it kindly. Gina is already hands-on, so she's fine, and Marco could move into something local, like helping councils buy services.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the consulting job for grocers involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd stop worrying and make a plan with dates in it, because a worry never paid anyone's mortgage. I'm guessing that's what I'd also say to myself.

say: I'd say five years is time to get ready and I'd start a working **group**.
I'd tell office friends to make a plan with **dates** in it.
think: I'd likely be **gone** by 61 before the hard part, but I'd keep tinkering.
I want to stay one of the people who can **explain** the tools.
do: Work **three more years**, build the forecasting tool properly and train the juniors.
Start small **consulting** for independent grocers using the tools.
Put money into my kids' house **deposit**.
feel: A bit **uneasy** and a bit excited at the slow burn.
S3.quote: With five years I'd stop worrying and make a plan with dates in it, because a worry never paid anyone's mortgage.
fieldNote: Sam uses the five years as a runway and has a clear sequence: work, consult, step back.
He is uneasy mainly for **Marco's** council job, not his own.
The consulting idea draws on real buying skills and is a credible side income.

steps.text: Work three more years, building the forecasting tool and training juniors
Start consulting for independent grocers who can't afford a buyer
Put money into Marco and Gina's house deposits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd shrug and say it's a long runway. I'd tell people that this is a decade of choices, and the sensible thing is to be curious and keep learning. I'd say online that the first thing to do is argue about who owns the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't hurt my job, I'd be gone in three years. It does matter for my kids' whole careers, and for the bit of me that likes being useful. I'd be calm for myself and watchful for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at 61 and use my time to build the small consulting thing, and maybe teach buying at the local college. I'd put savings in broad funds and a little in a friend's small greengrocers. I'd also join the council's working group on AI and jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a very long staircase. I'd be fine with it and I'd be a bit cheeky about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned teaching at the college. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college teaching is real. I know a lecturer, Pam, who runs the trade programme and she's wanted a practitioner for ages. I'd teach buyers to check software, which is something people will need whatever else happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the council working group do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long staircase, and I'd rather spend it teaching young buyers to check the machines than hiding from them. I'd want to be involved in that work.

say: I'd say ten years is a decade of **choices**, so be curious and keep learning.
I'd argue online about who **owns** the machines.
think: It won't hurt my own job, but it matters for my kids' **careers**.
I'm calm for myself and **watchful** for them.
do: Retire at **61** and build the small consulting work.
Teach buying at the local **college**, as lecturer Pam has asked.
Join the council's working group on AI and **jobs**.
feel: **Calm**, a long staircase, and a bit cheeky about it.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long staircase, and I'd rather spend it teaching young buyers to check the machines than hiding from them.
fieldNote: At ten years Sam is calm; his own career ends before the change bites.
His plan to teach checking skills at the **college** is concrete and named.
He still thinks about the political question of who owns the machines.

steps.text: Retire at 61 and build the small consulting work
Teach buyers to check software at the local college
Join the council's working group on AI and jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mostly for others. I could cope, but not everyone could, and there'd be no time to build safety nets. What would help is a basic income, retraining that's paid for, and firms telling us honestly what they plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, other than that I'm an optimist who worries. I'd rather spend my last working years teaching young buyers to check the machines than hiding from them.

headlineQuote: I'd rather spend my last working years teaching young buyers to check the machines than hiding from them.
portrait: Sam is **58**, a senior fruit and speciality buyer at Greenmarket Provisions, who already uses AI every day.
He's progressive and adaptive, so he moves first, builds his own tools and offers to **teach** colleagues.
With strong savings and a nearly paid house, he's calm in slow worlds and uneasy only in fast ones.
His worry is for friends, **colleagues** and his children, such as Marco in council planning, more than himself.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because others couldn't cope without safety nets.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income**, paid retraining and honest plans from employers.
